Female inshore lizardfish (Synodus foetens) reach an ultimate total length of 38 cm [Li = 38 cm], a size that is consistent with the moderate maximum lengths observed among benthic-dwelling members of the family Synodontidae. This asymptotic body size, derived from field measurements of the largest individuals, provides a useful benchmark for evaluating growth trajectories and reproductive potential within the population. The 38 cm [Li = 38 cm] total length places Synodus foetens among the intermediate-sized members of its genus, where maximum lengths typically range from 25 to 50 cm depending on geographic location and local environmental conditions. Comparative studies indicate that female inshore lizardfish from the northern Gulf of Mexico tend to reach slightly smaller ultimate lengths than those from the Caribbean, suggesting a latitudinal gradient in growth potential that may be mediated by temperature and prey availability. The observed value of 38 cm [Li = 38 cm] is derived from a comprehensive survey of adult specimens collected across multiple years, ensuring that the estimate reflects the true asymptotic size rather than an artifact of limited sampling. This moderate body size is accompanied by a correspondingly modest adult wet weight, as discussed below, and together these morphological traits underpin the species’ relatively rapid life history.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a comparatively modest body size, with females attaining puberty at a total length of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm]. The onset of reproductive capability at this length suggests that individuals may begin allocating resources toward gamete production well before approaching their ultimate body size, a strategy that may buffer against environmental variability. This early maturation may be particularly advantageous in variable environments where the probability of surviving to a larger size is uncertain. The total length at puberty of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm] is consistent with observations from other synodontids, such as Synodus intermedius, in which females similarly mature at around 40 to 50 percent of their maximum length.

Larval mortality rates during the yolk-sac stage are notoriously high in this family, with starvation being a primary source of loss if suitable prey such as copepod nauplii and rotifers are not encountered within the first few days after hatching.
